s: Vertex Inc DEF 14A filed 27 April 2026, beneficial ownership table as of 15 April 2026; VERX close 13.47 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 33,129,702 Class B plus 143,392 Class A = 33,273,094 shares (Class B converts one-for-one) x 13.47 = 448M. Proxy states sole voting and dispositive power; block sits in Westphal family trusts she controls.
did: Went to work at her father Ray Westphals sales-tax software company as a technical instructor, then finance and middle-market product, and joined the Vertex board in 1993; she and her sister kept dual-class control through the July 2020 Nasdaq IPO and she now holds 33.1 million Class B shares.
why: Vertex tax engines are wired into SAP and Oracle ERP installs and must be certified against roughly 13,000 US taxing jurisdictions, so ripping one out means re-certifying every rate table; the 2018 Wayfair ruling then forced every remote seller to calculate destination sales tax, widening the market overnight.
obst: Vertex stayed private for 42 years and the family had to build a dual-class Class B structure to list in 2020 without losing control; the 2024-2026 shift from on-premise licences to cloud subscriptions dragged reported revenue and VERX fell from 26.54 to about 13, halving the family stake.
turn: The June 2018 South Dakota v. Wayfair decision, which turned tax calculation from an option into a legal requirement for every online seller.

s: Vertex Inc DEF 14A filed 27 April 2026, beneficial ownership table as of 15 April 2026; VERX close 13.47 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 32,934,905 Class B plus 51,357 Class A = 32,986,262 shares x 13.47 = 444M. Proxy footnote 11 states sole voting and dispositive power over the Class B block.
did: Left a middle-market lending job at Chemical Bank to join her fathers tax-software company in 1991, served as its Treasurer and joined the board in 1993; she is one of the two sisters who between them control all 82 million Class B shares that carry voting control of Vertex.
why: Indirect tax is a compliance obligation, not a discretionary purchase, so Vertex bills recurring subscription revenue that customers cannot defer; staying private until 2020 let the family compound retained earnings, and the Class B structure meant the IPO raised cash without ceding the board.
obst: She joined a family firm in 1991 with a single mainframe product and no outside capital, and the company had to rebuild twice, first for client-server ERP in the 1990s and again for cloud after 2020, when the transition cut VERX to a 52-week low of 10.21.
turn: The 29 July 2020 Nasdaq listing, which put a public price on a 42-year-old private family business for the first time.

s: Bentley Systems DEF 14A filed 10 April 2026, ownership table as of 31 March 2026; BSY close 37.08 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,926,509 Class A plus 7,122,882 Class B = 9,049,391 shares (Class A converts one-for-one) x 37.08 = 336M. Excludes 26.7M shares in trusts he disclaims.
did: Founded Devon Systems International, a bond-trading software firm he sold to SunGard, then in 1991 joined the infrastructure-design software company his three brothers had built around MicroStation; he was President from 1996, CEO from 2000 to 2024, and took Bentley public on Nasdaq in September 2020.
why: Bentley sells to the owner-operators of roads, rail, water and power assets that last 50 years, so its ProjectWise and OpenRoads subscriptions renew at over 100 percent net retention; unlike Autodesk it never chased the volume CAD seat market, which let it stay private and cash-funded for 36 years.
obst: Four brothers ran the company without venture capital and nearly stalled in the late 1990s funding the move from desktop MicroStation into project collaboration; rather than sell out, Greg sold a minority stake to Siemens in 2016 to get a strategic partner and a valuation mark.
turn: The 23 September 2020 Nasdaq listing, which repriced a 36-year-old private engineering software company at more than 6 billion dollars.

s: Madrigal Pharmaceuticals DEF 14A filed 2026, ownership as of 1 April 2026, footnote 2; MDGL close 516.74 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 441,034 shares owned outright plus 242,914 options exercisable within 60 days = 683,948 x 516.74 = 353M gross of option strikes; her outright shares alone are 228M.
did: A tenured Penn genetics and medicine professor from 1987 to 2002 who ran metabolic research at Roche and Bristol-Myers Squibb, she co-founded Madrigal in 2011 to develop a shelved thyroid-hormone-receptor-beta agonist; that drug, resmetirom, became Rezdiffra, the first FDA-approved treatment for MASH in March 2024.
why: Rival NASH programmes attacked inflammation or fibrosis; Taub targeted the liver-selective thyroid receptor beta to burn intrahepatic fat, clearing steatohepatitis without the cardiac effects that killed earlier thyroid mimetics, and she ran the biopsy-endpoint trial the FDA required rather than a surrogate.
obst: Intercept was years ahead and widely assumed to win; Madrigal had to run MAESTRO-NASH, a 2,000-patient trial with paired liver biopsies, and the stock collapsed twice on ambiguous interim readouts before the endpoint data arrived.
turn: The 19 December 2022 MAESTRO-NASH topline, when resmetirom hit both biopsy endpoints and Madrigal shares roughly tripled in a single session.

s: SEI Investments DEF 14A 2026, ownership as of 12 March 2026, footnote 4; SEIC close 109.53 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,935,145 shares x 109.53 = 321M. Includes 57,750 exercisable options and 2,125,168 shares held by the Romeo 2012 Childrens Trust and 2019 GST Exempt Childrens Trust that he settled.
did: Left Arthur Andersen to become Treasurer and CFO of SEI in June 1979, when the Oaks, Pennsylvania firm was a small vendor of trust-accounting systems to banks; he was CFO to 1996 and an Executive Vice President to 2004, and still chairs the audit committee of the 13 billion dollar company he helped build.
why: SEI stopped licensing software to bank trust departments and ran the processing itself, turning one-time licence fees into multi-year outsourcing contracts with fixed software costs; that annuity plus four decades of buybacks compounded an early employees stake far past his salary.
obst: SEI began in 1968 as a maker of computer simulations to train bank loan officers and that business failed; Romeo joined during the pivot to trust accounting and had to fund the far more capital-hungry outsourcing model out of cash flow rather than equity.
turn: The 1980s decision to run banks trust back offices as a service instead of selling them the software.

s: Gaming and Leisure Properties DEF 14A 2026, ownership as of 2 April 2026, footnotes 1 and 2; GLPI close 43.55 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: Reported 10,795,408 GLPI shares less 4,708,917 held by the Carlino Family Trust and Residuary Trust for eight siblings = 6,086,491 x 43.55 = 265M. Excludes his residual PENN Entertainment holding.
did: Became CEO of Penn National Gaming in 1994 and took it public that year on the back of a single Pennsylvania racetrack, then rolled up tracks and casinos; in November 2013 he split the real estate out as Gaming and Leisure Properties, the first gaming REIT, and ran it as chairman and CEO.
why: Casino real estate trapped inside an operating company traded at gaming EBITDA multiples; moving it into a REIT let the same rent streams trade at real estate cap rates and escape corporate tax, while triple-net leases to Penn, Boyd, Bally's and Caesars pushed operating and capex risk onto the tenants.
obst: No gaming company had ever converted to a REIT and the IRS had never ruled on whether slot floors and casino buildings were qualifying real property; Carlino spent two years obtaining a private letter ruling and splitting 20 years of accounts into opco and propco.
turn: The 1 November 2013 spin-off of Gaming and Leisure Properties from Penn National Gaming.

s: Carpenter Technology DEF 14A filed August 2025, ownership table for the 2025 annual meeting; CRS close 492.38 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 501,267 shares beneficially owned plus 55,539 exercisable options = 556,806 x 492.38 = 274M, gross of option strikes.
did: Spent 22 years in finance at Alcoa, joined Carpenter Technology as CFO in 2013 and became CEO in July 2015; he rebuilt the specialty-alloy maker around aerospace and medical grades and its shares went from about 20 dollars in 2020 to 492 in August 2026.
why: Carpenter melts nickel, cobalt and titanium alloys qualified into specific jet-engine part numbers, and requalifying a new melter takes years; when air traffic returned after 2022 and engine makers could not get material, Carpenter could price a constrained melt capacity instead of chasing tonnage.
obst: COVID grounded aviation and Carpenter posted operating losses through fiscal 2021 and 2022 while customers destocked; Thene idled plants and cut headcount rather than fill furnaces with low-margin industrial bar, which meant defending negative earnings to shareholders for two years.
turn: The fiscal 2023 decision to allocate scarce melt capacity by margin per pound rather than by volume.

s: Forbes, Chloe Sorvino, 25 February 2026 feature on Misfits Market
m: Forbes states he is the single largest individual shareholder with an estimated 20 percent stake and worth at least 200 million, against a Forbes-estimated company valuation near 1 billion.
did: Founded Misfits Market in Philadelphia in 2018 at 26 after seeing unsold cosmetically imperfect apples at a Pennsylvania orchard, building a subscription box for rescued produce; it raised 526 million dollars, bought rival Imperfect Foods in 2022 and The Rounds in 2025, and now runs about 500 million in revenue.
why: Grocers reject produce on cosmetic specs, so that supply had no competing bidders; buying it direct from farms gave Misfits a structural gross-margin edge that Instacart and Amazon Fresh, buying at wholesale, cannot copy, and a subscription cadence made perishable logistics predictable.
obst: The 2022 online-grocery collapse killed most subscription grocers and cut the SoftBank-led 2 billion dollar 2021 valuation toward 1 billion; Misfits had to buy its largest competitor, merge two fulfilment networks and cut burn while subscriber growth stalled.
turn: The September 2022 acquisition of Imperfect Foods, which removed the only direct rival and doubled the customer base.

s: Essent Group DEF 14A filed 2026, beneficial ownership table, and director age table; ESNT close 68.07 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,481,544 shares x 68.07 = 169M, of which 472,106 are performance shares that vest only at maximum achievement, so the floor is about 137M.
did: After running Radian and then GMACs residential mortgage insurance units, he founded Essent in 2008 and raised roughly 500 million dollars from Goldman Sachs, Pine Brook and JPMorgan to start a private mortgage insurer with no legacy book while every incumbent was drowning in 2005-2007 loans; Essent listed in 2013.
why: Mortgage insurance is a function of loan vintage. Starting from zero in 2009 meant Essent wrote only post-crisis loans at 760 FICO scores while MGIC, Radian and Genworth were capital-impaired and unable to bid, letting a startup take share at the best underwriting moment in 40 years.
obst: Raising half a billion dollars of equity in 2008 and 2009 for a mortgage-related startup, and then convincing state regulators and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to approve an unproven counterparty with no claims history.
turn: The 2009 Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac approvals that let Essent write insurance on conforming loans.

s: Customers Bancorp DEF 14A 2026, ownership as of 1 April 2026, and director age table; CUBI close 79.79 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,984,611 shares plus 62,234 restricted stock units = 2,046,845 x 79.79 = 163M.
did: Ran Sovereign Bancorp from 1989 to 2006, growing it from about 500 million to 90 billion dollars of assets before losing a board fight over the Santander deal; in 2009 he recapitalised the failing New Century Bank in Pennsylvania, renamed it Customers Bank and built it to roughly 22 billion dollars of assets.
why: Customers ran almost no branches and used single-point-of-contact private bankers who each carried a book, so its efficiency ratio and deposit costs beat community banks with real estate; buying BankMobile and later building digital-payment deposit rails gave it low-cost funding that peers of its size could not source.
obst: Ousted from Sovereign in 2006 after Relational Investors forced out management over the Santander stake sale, he restarted at 57 by putting money into a small Pennsylvania bank operating under a regulatory agreement with negative tangible book momentum.
turn: The March 2023 collapse of Signature Bank and Silicon Valley Bank, when Customers took on billions in fleeing venture and digital-asset deposits and its shares re-rated.

s: Hamilton Lane DEF 14A 2026, ownership as of 13 July 2026, footnote 1; HLNE close 105.35 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 105,723 Class A plus 1,312,331 Class B units exchangeable one-for-one = 1,418,054 x 105.35 = 149M. Floor figure; excludes two decades of realised distributions and secondary sales.
did: A Philadelphia bank lawyer who was deputy general counsel of Fidelity Bank and general counsel of Industrial Valley Title, he joined the tiny private-markets advisory firm Hamilton Lane in 1993, became President in 1998 and CEO from 2001 to 2023, and took it public on Nasdaq in March 2017.
why: Public pensions want private-equity exposure but cannot staff diligence on hundreds of general partners; Hamilton Lane charges fees on committed capital across advisory, separate accounts and funds-of-funds, so revenue is contractual and grows with private-market allocations, not with equity prices.
obst: Hamilton Lane was a retainer-paid consultant with almost no discretionary assets; converting non-discretionary advisory relationships into fee-bearing mandates took most of a decade and a full fee-model rebuild before the business could carry a public listing.
turn: The March 2017 Nasdaq IPO, which put a public multiple on management fees the firm had been earning privately since the 1990s.

s: Hamilton Lane DEF 14A 2026, ownership as of 13 July 2026, footnote 2, and director age table; HLNE close 105.35 on stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 649,727 Class A plus 809,781 Class B units exchangeable one-for-one = 1,459,508 x 105.35 = 154M.
did: Joined Hamilton Lane in 1999 at 26 from the M&A desk at Brown Brothers Harriman, became Chief Investment Officer in 2003 at 30, then Vice Chairman, and has been Co-CEO since 2024; he built the firms data platform and its evergreen funds that sell private markets to wealth channels.
why: Institutional advisory fees are capped by what pensions will pay; Hirsch pushed the firm into evergreen semi-liquid vehicles distributed through wirehouses and RIAs, where the same underwriting earns full asset-management fees on a far larger pool of capital that had no other route into private equity.
obst: Wirehouse and RIA platforms had never distributed illiquid private-market products to retail clients; getting onto them required a semi-liquid structure regulators would accept and years of platform diligence before a single dollar of retail money arrived.
turn: The 2020-2021 launch of the Hamilton Lane Private Assets Fund and the evergreen platform that followed it.
